newsitem.title: USA: Dole raps'liberal' Clinton; Perot files debate suit.
newsitem.headline: Dole raps'liberal' Clinton; Perot files debate suit.

text.p: Bob Dole hammered President Bill Clinton's alleged "liberal" record on Monday, while Clinton unleashed a television ad targeting Dole's record and Ross Perot filed suit to join the two in campaign debates.

"President Clinton came to town a liberal," Dole, the Republican presidential candidate, told a rally in suburban Washington, hitting the same angle for the second day. "He's still a liberal. The only thing that stopped him in his tracks was (the people) electing a Republican Congress in 1994."
Dole trailed Clinton by a double-digit margin in most polls, but brushed aside his underdog status saying, "I don't believe in polls. If I did, I wouldn't be able to sleep at night."
Monday's CNN/USA Today/Gallup daily tracking poll showed Clinton getting 53 percent, Dole with 36 percent and Reform Party candidate Perot with 5 percent. The margin of error was 4 percent.

However, Democrat Clinton said in an interview to be televised on Monday evening that he was ignoring polls that show him with a commanding lead because the "weight of history" is against the re-election of a Democrat to the White House.

"I try not to think about the polls, except it's better to be ahead than behind, but the most important thing is to work like crazy until the end," Clinton told the PBS programme "The Newshour with Jim Lehrer".
Clinton brushed aside Dole's charges of liberal bias, saying his record refuted the accusation, notably on such issues as welfare reform, crime and deficit reduction.
At the same time, Clinton's campaign released a tough advertisement aimed at making Dole look old and out of touch, while stressing the Kansas Republican's long Washington tenure.

"Let's go back in time," the ad begins, then notes Dole's votes against Medicare in the 1960s, the Education Department in the 1970s, the office of the White House drug czar in the 1980s and the Family and Medical Leave Act in the 1990s.

Clinton himself played the trump card available to all presidential incumbents: he stayed at the White House and acted presidential, issuing a reassuring statement on the impact of Russian President Boris Yeltsin's health problems and signing a $265.6 billion defence bill.

Meanwhile lawyers for Perot and his running mate, economist Pat Choate, filed papers in federal court in Washington seeking an injunction to force their inclusion in presidential and vice presidential debates scheduled for next month.

The lawyers said they hoped a judge would hold a hearing on their suit this week. They would argue that Perot's constitutional rights were violated when the Commission on Presidential Debates decided the Texas billionaire should not be included because he had no chance of being elected.

The Dole and Clinton camps agreed to hold two one-on-one televised presidential debates between their candidates on Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and Oct. 16 in San Diego. A vice presidential debate was scheduled for Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.
